title: Uniform partial Fourier decay for compact spatial symbol families
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field], Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure. Let $m,d\geq1$, $p,q\geq0$ and $r\in\mathbf Z$. Let $b(x,z,\xi)$ be a smooth complex $q\times p$ matrix on $\mathbf R^d\times\mathbf R^m\times\mathbf R^m$. Suppose $b$ vanishes outside $L_x\times L_z$ in $(x,z)$, for fixed compact sets $L_x,L_z$, and for all multi-indices $\alpha,\gamma,\beta$ one has $\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_z^\gamma\partial_\xi^\beta b(x,z,\xi)\|\leq C_{\alpha\gamma\beta}(1+|\xi|)^{r-|\beta|}$. Define the absolutely convergent partial Fourier integral $$B(x,\eta,\xi)=(2\pi)^{-m}\int_{\mathbf R^m}e^{-iz\cdot\eta}b(x,z,\xi)\,dz.$$ Then $B$ is jointly smooth, vanishes for $x\notin L_x$, and for every $\alpha,\delta,\beta$ and integer $L\geq0$ there is $C'_{\alpha\delta\beta L}<\infty$ such that $$\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\eta^\delta\partial_\xi^\beta B(x,\eta,\xi)\|\leq C'_{\alpha\delta\beta L}(1+|\eta|)^{-L}(1+|\xi|)^{r-|\beta|}.$$ The mixed derivative equals the integral obtained by applying $\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta$ to $b$ and multiplying the integrand by $(-iz)^\delta$. For fixed indices and fixed support sets, $C'$ can be bounded by a constant times a finite sum of the input constants $C_{\alpha\gamma\beta}$ (with finitely many $\gamma$); in particular these estimates are uniform for a family with common supports and common input bounds.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, (3.4)–(3.5), Proposition 3.7, printed pp.12–13. Agent-supplied parameter version of the compact-spatial Fourier-decay calculation; supplemental Demailly course pseudodiff.pdf, §3, (3.11) and the estimates after (3.15), printed pp.9–11, read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf. The course gives the method, not this full parameter statement.

proof.text: If $p=0$ or $q=0$, the matrix space is zero and every assertion holds with $C'=0$; hence assume both positive. Put $t=(x,\eta,\xi)$ and $a(t,z)=e^{-iz\cdot\eta}b(x,z,\xi)$. Every derivative of $b$ is zero off $L_x\times L_z$: its complement is open and $b$ is identically zero there. Thus each matrix entry of every derivative of $a$ in $(t,z)$ is smooth and supported in $L_z$ as a function of $z$. Apply the continuous-compact-support integrability statement entrywise. The entrywise bounds give an integrable majorant of the matrix norm, so $B$ is absolutely convergent by the majorant statement. Writing the integrand as $\sum_k h_k(z)c_k$ in a fixed real basis $(c_k)$ of the matrix space, additivity and the scalar-function clause $\int h(z)c\,dz=(\int h)c$ of the Euclidean Bochner-calculus statement show that the matrix integral is computed entrywise. If $x\notin L_x$ its integrand is zero and $B=0$.

proof.text: Fix a parameter point $t_0$ and a bounded open ball $U$ about it with compact closure. For every $n\geq0$ the real parameter derivative $D_t^n a(t,z)$ is a finite array of smooth compactly supported entries, hence is measurable and integrable in $z$ at fixed $t$. Its next derivative has norm bounded by $M_n\mathbf1_{L_z}(z)$ for all $t\in U$: differentiating the exponential produces only monomials in the bounded variable $z\in L_z$, and the symbol bounds on the bounded $\xi$-projection of $U$ bound the remaining factors. All norms on these finite arrays are bounded by fixed multiples of the sum of entry norms. The constant function $1$ on $L_z$ is integrable by the compact-set statement, so $M_n\mathbf1_{L_z}$ is an integrable real majorant. Apply the dominated Fréchet-derivative theorem with $H=\mathbf R^{d+2m}$ and codomain the finite-dimensional real space of $n$-linear maps into the matrix space. Its derivative bound holds simultaneously on $U$, and its measurability and integrability hypotheses hold by the preceding observations. Therefore $I_n(t)=\int D_t^n a(t,z)\,dz$ is differentiable, with derivative $I_{n+1}(t)$ under the usual identification of multilinear maps; this identification is a real-linear isomorphism of finite-dimensional spaces, which commutes with the integral by the coordinatewise computation of step 1.

proof.text: Each $I_n$ is continuous because it is differentiable by step 2. Starting from $D^0 I_0=I_0$, induction gives $D^n I_0=I_n$ for every $n$; the inductive step is precisely $D I_n=I_{n+1}$ proved there. Hence $B=(2\pi)^{-m}I_0$ is jointly smooth. Evaluation of a multilinear derivative on fixed coordinate vectors is a finite coordinate linear combination, so the coordinatewise computation of the integral (additivity and the scalar-function clause of the Euclidean Bochner-calculus statement) moves those evaluations through the integral. Direct differentiation of $a$ now gives, with $c=(2\pi)^{-m}$, $$\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\eta^\delta\partial_\xi^\beta B=c\int e^{-iz\cdot\eta}f_{x,\xi}(z)\,dz,\qquad f_{x,\xi}(z)=(-iz)^\delta\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta b(x,z,\xi).$$ The exponential is independent of $x,\xi$, and its $\eta$-derivative is $(-iz)^\delta$ times itself, so no extra terms occur.

proof.text: Fix $x,\xi,\eta$. For each entry $h$ of $f_{x,\xi}$ and coordinate $j$, apply the integration-by-parts statement with $f(z)=e^{-iz\cdot\eta}$, $g(z)=h(z)$ and direction $e_j$. Both factors are smooth everywhere; $fg$, $(D f[e_j])g$ and $f(D g[e_j])$ are continuous compactly supported functions, hence meet its three integrability hypotheses. Since $D f[e_j]=-i\eta_j f$, it gives $\int e^{-iz\cdot\eta}\partial_j h\,dz=i\eta_j\int e^{-iz\cdot\eta}h\,dz$. Apply this identity again to $\partial_j h$ to get the multiplier $-\eta_j^2$ for $\partial_j^2 h$. Set $\Delta_z=\sum_j\partial_j^2$. By finite integral linearity, the identity for $1-\Delta_z$ has multiplier $1+|\eta|^2$. Iterating it $N$ times is valid because every intervening derivative is still smooth with support in $L_z$. Thus, entrywise and hence as matrices, $$ (1+|\eta|^2)^N\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\eta^\delta\partial_\xi^\beta B=c\int e^{-iz\cdot\eta}(1-\Delta_z)^N f_{x,\xi}(z)\,dz.$$

proof.text:
Expand $(1-\Delta_z)^N$ as a finite linear combination of $\partial_z^
u$ with $|
u|\leq2N$, and apply Leibniz to $\partial_z^
u(z^\delta\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^ eta b)$. Its terms have the form a fixed coefficient times $z^{\delta-\kappa}\partial_x^\alpha\partial_z^{
u-\kappa}\partial_\xi^ eta b$, with $\kappa\leq
u,\delta$. Choose $R\geq1$ with $|z|\leq R$ on $L_z$. The polynomial factors have norm at most $R^{|\delta|}$ there. Consequently, for a finite constant $A_{m,N,\delta,R}$ depending only on the displayed indices and $L_z$, $$\|(1-\Delta_z)^Nf_{x,\xi}(z)\|\leq A_{m,N,\delta,R}\sum_{|\gamma|\leq2N}C_{\alpha\gamma eta}(1+|\xi|)^{r-| eta|}\mathbf1_{L_z}(z).$$ Let $v_z=\int_{L_z}1\,dz<\infty$, supplied by the compact-set integrability statement. The vector majorant estimate applied to step 4 yields $$\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\eta^\delta\partial_\xi^ eta B\|\leq c v_z A_{m,N,\delta,R}\Big(\sum_{|\gamma|\leq2N}C_{\alpha\gamma eta}\Big)(1+|\eta|^2)^{-N}(1+|\xi|)^{r-| eta|}.$$

proof.text: Given $L\geq0$, choose $N=\lceil L/2\rceil$. For $u\geq0$, $(1+u)^2\leq2(1+u^2)$ and $2N\geq L$ imply $(1+u^2)^{-N}\leq2^N(1+u)^{-L}$. Step 5 therefore gives the desired constant $$C'_{\alpha\delta\beta L}=2^Nc v_z A_{m,N,\delta,R}\sum_{|\gamma|\leq2N}C_{\alpha\gamma\beta}.$$ Input bound constants may be taken nonnegative, as their bounding inequalities already require. This formula uses only the indicated finite list of spatial symbol bounds. It is independent of $x,\eta,\xi$ and of the member of a family with common supports and common input bounds. Empty support sets give the zero function; $L=0$ uses $N=0$. Negative $r$ causes no change because $1+|\xi|$ is strictly positive.
